In This Video

Treatment of Asthma Exacerbation according to GINA Guidelines

Asthma exacerbation definition

Patient classification in ER into Mild/Moderate, Severe or Life threatening

  • Asthma exacerbation management
  • Features in patients with higher risk for asthma related death

Asthma Exacerbation

A flare up or exacerbation is an acute (or subacute) worsening in symptoms and lung function from the patient’s usual status; this maybe the initial presentation of asthma

Management of Asthma Exacerbation

Start the patient on SABA and oxygen

Then classify the patient into mild/moderate or severe or life threatening asthma exacerbation by assessing exacerbation severity through:

If the patient able to speak sentences or only words

Respiratory rate, pulse rate, oxygen saturation and lung function (e.g. PEF)

Note potential over estimation of pulse oximetry readings in patients with dark skin color

Start the patient on SABA and oxygen

Then classify the patient by assessing exacerbation severity through:

If the patient able to speak sentences or only words

Respiratory rate, pulse rate, oxygen saturation and lung function (e.g. PEF)

Note potential over estimation of pulse oximetry readings in patients with dark skin color

Consider differential diagnosis: anaphylaxis, uncompensated heart failure, inhaled foreign body or pulmonary embolism

Patients with mild/moderate exacerbation can be started on early OCS, in addition to the oxygen and SABA; check response of symptoms and saturation frequently and measure lung function after 1 hour

In patients with severe or life threatening exacerbations immediately give inhaled SABA, inhaled ipratropium bromide, oxygen and systemic corticosteroids; then Transfer to acute care facility or ICU

Titrate oxygen to a target of 93-95% in adults and adolescents +12 and 94-98% in children 6-11

If the patient has inadequate response to the previous measures, then intravenous magnesium sulfate should be considered

Don’t routinely perform chest X rays, blood gases; Don’t routinely prescribe antibiotics for asthma exacerbations

Don’t use sedatives

Inhaled albuterol is what most commonly used for bronchodilation; but studies have shown similar efficacy for budesonide- formoterol

Patient classification in Asthma Exacerbations

  • Patients classified into Mild/Moderate, Severe and Life threatening Asthma exacerbations
  • Patient with Mild/Moderate asthma exacerbation:
  • Talks in phrases, prefers sitting to lying, not agitated
  • Respiratory rate increased but < 30
  • Accessory muscles are not used
  • Pulse rate 100- 120 bpm
  • O2 saturation is 90- 95% on air
  • PEF > 50% of the predicted or best
  • Patient with Severe asthma exacerbation:
  • Talks in words, sits in tripod position (hunched forward), agitated
  • Respiratory rate > 30
  • Accessory muscles are in use
  • Pulse rate > 120 bpm
  • O2 saturation is < 90% on air
  • PEF < 50% of the predicted or best
  • Patients with life threatening asthma exacerbation: drowsy, confused or silent chest

Monitoring and discharge

Patient monitored frequently for response

Patient assessed for discharge if symptoms improved, SABA not needed, PEF improving > 60-80% of personal best or predicted, oxygen saturation > 94% on room air and if the home resources are adequate

Asthma Related Death

Risk of asthma related death is higher in patients with specific features, those features include:

  • Features in patient History
  • History of near fatal asthma requiring intubation and ventilation
  • Hospitalization or emergency care for asthma in the last year
  • Features related to Medications
  • Patient not currently using ICS, or with poor adherence to ICS
  • Currently using or recently stopped OCS (recent severity)
  • Over use of SABA (> 200 doses per month)

Risk of asthma related death is higher in patients with specific features, those features include:

  • Features related to patient comorbidities
  • History of psychiatric disease or psychosocial problems (means patient not compliant to treatment)
  • Confirmed food allergy in asthma patient
  • Other comorbidities such as infections (e.g. pneumonia), diabetes or heart disease
  • Lack of a written asthma action plan
